steps.prompt: What decides whether you use to + verb or verb + -ing?
options: The first verb — each verb takes one pattern.
Whether the sentence is positive or negative.
steps.answer: The first verb — each verb takes one pattern.
steps.why: There is no rule of meaning. Decide takes to; enjoy takes -ing. You learn them with the verb.

steps.title: Which pattern does the verb take?
steps.html:
verb + to + base formverb + -ing
decide to change careerenjoy working at the weekend
want to have childrenstop thinking about it
hope to pass the examskeep working four days a week
plan to retire in Junedon’t mind starting late
learn to swimfinish studying
need / would like to talkgive up / can’t stand waiting

+ to: decide, want, hope, plan, need, learn, would like, expect, promise, choose, offer, agree.

+ -ing: enjoy, stop, keep, finish, give up, don’t mind, can’t stand, regret, take up, look forward to.

A few verbs take both with almost the same meaning: start, begin, continue, like, love, hate. He began studying law = He began to study law.

After a preposition, always use -ing: She is interested in working abroad. He is tired of waiting.

You met the -ing form after like / love / can’t stand in Lesson 3. It comes back as a full topic in Unit 10.

steps.title: You are going to read about three people who changed something big.
steps.sub: At what age do you think people usually change career? There is no wrong answer here.

steps.title: Three people who changed direction
steps.sub: Three people, three ages, three decisions.
steps.html:
Reading

Nobody plans to change direction. It happens when one thing stops working and another starts to look possible.

Bakyt was a teenager when he decided to become a doctor, and he did. He worked in a hospital in Almaty for eleven years. Then, at thirty-four, he stopped enjoying the work. “I didn’t hate it,” he says. “I just stopped looking forward to Mondays.” He took up photography at the weekend, and two years later he changed career completely. He now photographs food for restaurants. “I don’t regret studying medicine. It taught me how to deal with people.”

Renata left home at eighteen and never wanted to have children. At forty-one she got married, and at forty-three she had a baby. “People expect you to decide these things at twenty-five,” she says. “I decided at forty-two. I don’t mind starting late — I know exactly why I am doing it.” She kept working as an architect and now works four days a week.

Amir passed his exams at sixty-one and began studying law. He retired from his engineering job the year before, and he could not stop thinking about the courses he never took. He is now in his sixties and in his third year. “My children think it’s funny,” he says. “But I don’t want to spend twenty years doing nothing.”

Three people, three ages. None of them planned it. All of them chose it.

steps.title: Choose the best answer.
steps.prompt: What do the three people have in common?
options: None of them planned the change, but all of them chose it.
All of them changed direction at roughly the same age.
All of them now regret the decision that they made.
steps.answer: None of them planned the change, but all of them chose it.
steps.why: The last line: “None of them planned it. All of them chose it.”
